questions.q: Why does Theo write both AKS and the AWS backup infrastructure into one Terraform project instead of two separate ones?
options: Terraform doesn't support multiple projects
One shared project with shared remote state means a terraform plan surfaces drift on either cloud in the same review, preventing the two sides of the architecture from quietly drifting apart
It's required by Azure's terms of service
To reduce the number of HCL files to exactly one
questions.explain: The multi-provider pattern turns Lesson 3's architecture diagram from a picture into something enforced in code — nobody can change the AWS backup side without it showing up alongside AKS changes.

questions.q: What does the remote state backend configuration do, and why does it matter more with two providers involved?
options: It speeds up terraform apply
It stores shared, locked state outside any one engineer's machine, preventing two engineers from applying conflicting changes to either cloud at once — with twice the blast radius if skipped
It automatically fixes HCL syntax errors
It's only needed for the AWS provider, not Azure
questions.explain: State locking prevents concurrent conflicting applies; with two cloud providers in one project, skipping it doubles the risk surface.

questions.q: What does the aws_backup Terraform module provision?
options: A second, fully live AKS-equivalent Kubernetes cluster
The cross-region-replicated S3 bucket and the standby RDS read replica from the Lesson 3 architecture diagram, which stay idle under normal operation
The checkout-api Deployment and HPA
The Grafana FinOps dashboard
questions.explain: The AWS side stays backup/DR as established in Lesson 3 — replicated storage and a standby database replica, now codified instead of manually set up.

questions.q: Which two things does this lesson deliberately keep OUT of Terraform's management for this phase?
options: The AKS cluster and the remote state backend
Kubernetes-level objects (Deployments, Services, HPAs) and the FinOps dashboard — both left as plain kubectl YAML or direct Grafana/Azure Monitor config
The AWS provider entirely
Nothing is excluded; everything is in Terraform
questions.explain: App-level Kubernetes objects stay as kubectl-applied YAML, and the dashboard is deployed directly in Grafana/Azure Monitor — both deliberate scoping decisions given the deadline, not oversights.

questions.q: What is the real benefit of expressing Lesson 3's architecture as Terraform code rather than leaving it as a one-time manual setup?
options: It makes the architecture diagram unnecessary
It can be planned, reviewed, and reapplied consistently, and drift on either cloud becomes visible rather than silently accumulating
It eliminates the need for an AWS account
It automatically scales checkout-api
questions.explain: Codifying both clouds means the architecture is enforced and auditable through terraform plan/apply, instead of depending on someone's memory of a manual setup.
